queries.name: customer_segments
queries.question: Consumer, Corporate and Home Office are DataCo's three segments. Segment value per order and per customer is the comparison that matters.
queries.sql:
-- Consumer, Corporate and Home Office are DataCo's three segments. Segment
-- value per order and per customer is the comparison that matters.
SELECT
    c.customer_segment                                       AS segment,
    count(DISTINCT c.customer_id)                           AS customers,
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id)                               AS orders,
    round(sum(o.order_sales), 2)                             AS sales,
    round(sum(o.order_profit), 2)                            AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(o.order_profit) / sum(o.order_sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    round(sum(o.order_sales) / count(DISTINCT o.order_id), 2) AS avg_order_sales,
    round(sum(o.order_sales) / count(DISTINCT c.customer_id), 2) AS sales_per_customer
FROM dataco.orders o
JOIN dataco.customers c USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sales DESC;

queries.name: discount_vs_margin
queries.question: Does discounting actually pay? Buckets order lines by the discount they carried so the relationship can be read without assuming one exists.
queries.sql:
-- Does discounting actually pay? Buckets order lines by the discount they
-- carried so the relationship can be read without assuming one exists.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <= 0.00 THEN '1. no discount'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.15 THEN '2. 1-14% off'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.20 THEN '3. 15-19% off'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.30 THEN '4. 20-29% off'
        WHEN order_item_discount_rate <  0.50 THEN '5. 30-49% off'
        ELSE                              '6. 50%+ off'
    END                                                      AS discount_band,
    count(*)                                                 AS order_lines,
    round(avg(order_item_discount_rate), 4)                 AS avg_discount_rate,
    round(sum(sales), 2)                                     AS sales,
    round(sum(order_profit_per_order), 2)                    AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_profit_per_order) / sum(sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    round(avg(order_item_profit_ratio), 4)                  AS avg_profit_ratio
FROM dataco.order_items
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: loss_making_orders
queries.question: Orders that lost money outright. If an operations review only looks at totals these disappear inside an average; counting them makes them arguable.
queries.sql:
-- Orders that lost money outright. If an operations review only looks at totals
-- these disappear inside an average; counting them makes them arguable.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN order_profit >= 0    THEN '1. profitable or break-even'
        WHEN order_profit > -100  THEN '2. small loss (0 to -100)'
        WHEN order_profit > -500  THEN '3. moderate loss (-100 to -500)'
        ELSE                           '4. large loss (below -500)'
    END                                                      AS profit_band,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)      AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS sales,
    round(sum(order_profit), 2)                              AS profit,
    min(order_profit)                                        AS worst_single_order
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: margin_by_department
queries.question: The central profitability question. DataCo is widely reported to be close to break-even overall; this shows whether that is uniform or hides a mix shift.
queries.sql:
-- The central profitability question. DataCo is widely reported to be close to
-- break-even overall; this shows whether that is uniform or hides a mix shift.
SELECT
    p.department_name                                        AS department,
    count(DISTINCT p.product_card_id)                        AS products,
    count(*)                                                 AS order_lines,
    round(sum(i.sales), 2)                                   AS sales,
    round(sum(i.order_profit_per_order), 2)                  AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(i.order_profit_per_order) / sum(i.sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    round(sum(i.order_item_discount), 2)                     AS discount_given,
    round(100.0 * sum(i.order_item_discount) / sum(i.sales), 2) AS discount_pct
FROM dataco.order_items i
JOIN dataco.products p USING (product_card_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sales DESC;

queries.name: order_flow_by_month
queries.question: How did order volume and value move month by month? DataCo is a 2-year window, so this shows both the level and whether the business was growing.
queries.sql:
-- How did order volume and value move month by month? DataCo is a 2-year
-- window, so this shows both the level and whether the business was growing.
SELECT
    to_char(date_trunc('month', order_date), 'YYYY-MM')     AS month,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    count(DISTINCT customer_id)                              AS customers,
    round(sum(order_value), 2)                               AS order_value,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS order_sales,
    round(sum(order_profit), 2)                              AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_profit) / sum(order_sales), 2)   AS margin_pct,
    round(avg(total_quantity), 2)                            AS avg_units_per_order
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: order_status_mix
queries.question: Not every order completed, and the ones that did not are where the money quietly disappears. Reports value by terminal status.
queries.sql:
-- Not every order completed, and the ones that did not are where the money
-- quietly disappears. Reports value by terminal status.
SELECT
    order_status,
    delivery_status,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)      AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS sales,
    round(sum(order_profit), 2)                              AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_profit) / sum(order_sales), 2)  AS margin_pct
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY orders DESC;

queries.name: revenue_by_market
queries.question: DataCo is a multinational. Market share shows how concentrated the operation is geographically before any per-country drill-down.
queries.sql:
-- DataCo is a multinational. Market share shows how concentrated the operation
-- is geographically before any per-country drill-down.
SELECT
    market,
    count(DISTINCT order_region)                             AS regions,
    count(DISTINCT order_country)                            AS countries,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(sum(order_sales), 2)                               AS sales,
    round(100.0 * sum(order_sales) / sum(sum(order_sales)) OVER (), 2)
                                                              AS pct_of_sales,
    round(avg(shipping_delay_days), 2)                       AS avg_delay_days,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_late) / count(*), 2) AS pct_late
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY sales DESC;

queries.name: shipping_performance
queries.question: DataCo publishes a promise (days_for_shipment_scheduled) and an outcome (days_for_shipping_real). This measures the gap, by shipping mode.
queries.sql:
-- DataCo publishes a promise (days_for_shipment_scheduled) and an outcome
-- (days_for_shipping_real). This measures the gap, by shipping mode.
SELECT
    shipping_mode,
    count(*)                                                 AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_late) / count(*), 2) AS pct_late,
    round(avg(days_for_shipment_scheduled), 2)              AS avg_days_promised,
    round(avg(days_for_shipping_real), 2)                   AS avg_days_actual,
    round(avg(shipping_delay_days), 2)                      AS avg_delay_days,
    round(avg(lead_time_days)::numeric, 2)                  AS avg_lead_time_days,
    max(shipping_delay_days)                                 AS worst_delay_days
FROM dataco.orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY orders DESC;

queries.name: worst_categories_by_margin
queries.question: The bottom of the margin table. A category can be high-volume and still lose money on every unit, which no revenue ranking would reveal.
queries.sql:
-- The bottom of the margin table. A category can be high-volume and still lose
-- money on every unit, which no revenue ranking would reveal.
SELECT
    p.category_name                                          AS category,
    p.department_name                                        AS department,
    count(DISTINCT p.product_card_id)                        AS products,
    count(*)                                                 AS order_lines,
    round(sum(i.sales), 2)                                   AS sales,
    round(sum(i.order_profit_per_order), 2)                  AS profit,
    round(100.0 * sum(i.order_profit_per_order) / sum(i.sales), 2) AS margin_pct,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE i.order_profit_per_order < 0)     AS lines_losing_money
FROM dataco.order_items i
JOIN dataco.products p USING (product_card_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2
HAVING sum(i.sales) > 0
ORDER BY margin_pct ASC
LIMIT 12;

queries.name: campaign_performance
queries.question: Dunn & Bradstreet ran 30 named campaigns. The control group matters: comparing contacted households against the panel AVERAGE is not a control at all, because campaigns were aimed at frequent shoppers, so the contacted group is pre-loaded with high spenders. This compares each campaign's contacted households against the households that were NEVER contacted by anything. WITH household_spend AS (
queries.sql:
-- Dunn & Bradstreet ran 30 named campaigns. The control group matters: comparing
-- contacted households against the panel AVERAGE is not a control at all, because
-- campaigns were aimed at frequent shoppers, so the contacted group is pre-loaded
-- with high spenders. This compares each campaign's contacted households against
-- the households that were NEVER contacted by anything.
WITH household_spend AS (
    SELECT household_key, sum(sales_value) AS spend
    FROM dunnhumby.transactions
    GROUP BY 1
),
ever_contacted AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT household_key FROM dunnhumby.campaign_contacts
),
control AS (
    SELECT avg(spend) AS avg_control_spend, count(*) AS control_households
    FROM household_spend h
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ever_contacted e WHERE e.household_key = h.household_key)
)
SELECT
    c.campaign,
    c.description                                            AS campaign_name,
    (c.end_day - c.start_day)                                AS duration_days,
    count(DISTINCT cc.household_key)                         AS households_contacted,
    round(avg(h.spend), 2)                                   AS avg_spend_contacted,
    (SELECT round(avg_control_spend, 2) FROM control)        AS avg_spend_never_contacted,
    round(avg(h.spend) - (SELECT avg_control_spend FROM control), 2)
                                                           AS lift_vs_never_contacted
FROM dunnhumby.campaigns c
JOIN dunnhumby.campaign_contacts cc ON cc.campaign = c.campaign
JOIN household_spend h ON h.household_key = cc.household_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY households_contacted DESC;

queries.name: coupon_redemption
queries.question: Coupons were sent far more often than they were redeemed. The gap between coupons issued and redemptions is the redemption rate that actually matters.
queries.sql:
-- Coupons were sent far more often than they were redeemed. The gap between
-- coupons issued and redemptions is the redemption rate that actually matters.
--
-- coupons has 119,384 rows over only 1,135 distinct coupon_upc values, so
-- joining it to the 2,318 redemption rows on coupon_upc alone multiplies the
-- two together and reports millions of redemptions that never happened. Each
-- side is therefore aggregated to coupon_upc BEFORE the join.
WITH issued AS (
    SELECT
        coupon_upc,
        count(*)                       AS product_campaign_rows,
        count(DISTINCT campaign)       AS campaigns,
        count(DISTINCT product_id)     AS products
    FROM dunnhumby.coupons
    GROUP BY 1
),
redeemed AS (
    SELECT
        coupon_upc,
        count(*)                       AS redemption_rows,
        count(DISTINCT household_key)  AS households_redeeming
    FROM dunnhumby.coupon_redemptions
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    count(*)                                                  AS coupons_defined,
    count(r.coupon_upc)                                       AS coupons_ever_redeemed,
    round(100.0 * count(r.coupon_upc) / count(*), 2)          AS pct_of_coupons_redeemed,
    COALESCE(sum(r.redemption_rows), 0)                       AS redemption_rows,
    COALESCE(sum(r.households_redeeming), 0)                  AS households_redeeming,
    sum(issued.product_campaign_rows)                         AS product_campaign_rows_issued
FROM issued
LEFT JOIN redeemed r USING (coupon_upc);

queries.name: demographic_coverage_gap
queries.question: The headline data-quality finding for this source. transaction_data.csv names 2,500 distinct households; hh_demographic.csv names only 801, and the file is byte-identical to the copy inside the publisher's own zip, so this is the publisher's coverage and not a truncated download. Any demographic split is therefore a minority-sample split and has to be described as one.
queries.sql:
-- The headline data-quality finding for this source. transaction_data.csv names
-- 2,500 distinct households; hh_demographic.csv names only 801, and the file
-- is byte-identical to the copy inside the publisher's own zip, so this is the
-- publisher's coverage and not a truncated download. Any demographic split is
-- therefore a minority-sample split and has to be described as one.
SELECT
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT household_key) FROM dunnhumby.transactions)
                                                           AS households_transacting,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.households)             AS households_with_demographics,
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT t.household_key) FROM dunnhumby.transactions t
       WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dunnhumby.households h
                         WHERE h.household_key = t.household_key))
                                                           AS households_missing_demographics,
    round(100.0 * (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.households)
          / (SELECT count(DISTINCT household_key) FROM dunnhumby.transactions), 2)
                                                           AS pct_with_demographics,
    round(100.0 * (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.households)
          / (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.household_rfm), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_rfm_households_described;

queries.name: discount_composition
queries.question: Retailer discounts versus manufacturer coupons. Splitting them shows who is actually funding the promotion, which a single discount total cannot.
queries.sql:
-- Retailer discounts versus manufacturer coupons. Splitting them shows who is
-- actually funding the promotion, which a single discount total cannot.
--
-- SIGN CONVENTION, measured not assumed. This source stores signs two different
-- ways and both are real:
--   * retail_disc / coupon_disc keep the RAW sign: a discount is NEGATIVE.
--     retail_disc is negative on 1,303,026 of 2,595,732 lines (min -180,
--     max +3.99); coupon_disc is negative on 36,422 lines (min -55.93, max 0).
--   * total_discount was normalised during ETL to a POSITIVE magnitude:
--     1,319,391 lines are > 0 (max 180) and only 10 lines are < 0.
-- Bucketing therefore has to test retail_disc/coupon_disc for "< 0", not
-- total_discount for "> 0", or every line lands in "no discount".
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN retail_disc < 0 AND coupon_disc < 0 THEN '1. retailer and coupon together'
        WHEN retail_disc < 0                     THEN '2. retailer discount only'
        WHEN coupon_disc < 0                     THEN '3. manufacturer coupon only'
        ELSE                                         '4. no discount at all'
    END                                                       AS discount_type,
    count(*)                                                 AS basket_lines,
    round(sum(gross_sales_value), 2)                         AS gross_sales,
    round(abs(sum(total_discount)), 2)                       AS discount_given,
    round(100.0 * abs(sum(total_discount)) / sum(gross_sales_value), 2) AS effective_discount_pct,
    round(abs(sum(retail_disc))::numeric, 2)                 AS retailer_funded,
    round(abs(sum(coupon_disc))::numeric, 2)                 AS manufacturer_funded,
    round(100.0 * abs(sum(coupon_disc)::numeric) / NULLIF(abs(sum(total_discount)), 0), 2)
                                                           AS pct_funded_by_manufacturer
FROM dunnhumby.transactions
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: exposure_grid_density
queries.question: Why the query above has to restrict. Most of the 36.8 million row exposure grid corresponds to no sale in that product, store and week at all.
queries.sql:
-- Why the query above has to restrict. Most of the 36.8 million row exposure
-- grid corresponds to no sale in that product, store and week at all.
SELECT
    count(*)                                                 AS exposure_rows,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NOT NULL)         AS rows_matching_a_sale,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NULL)             AS rows_with_no_sale,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NULL) / count(*), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_grid_with_no_sale
FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure p
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT DISTINCT product_id, store_id, week_no FROM dunnhumby.transactions
) s USING (product_id, store_id, week_no);

queries.name: exposure_vs_sales
queries.question: Do products that appear on display actually sell more?
queries.sql:
-- Do products that appear on display actually sell more?
--
-- Two traps here, both measured rather than guessed. First, promo_exposure is a
-- dense product x store x week grid: 36.8 million rows, and 98.9% of those
-- product-store-weeks have NO matching transaction at all. Comparing averages
-- across the whole grid compares mostly zeros, which says nothing about display.
-- Second, a display comparison over the whole grid also mixes in the fact that
-- retailers promote things they already expect to sell, so any gap is an
-- association and not a causal lift. The query therefore restricts to the
-- product-store-weeks that actually sold, and says so.
WITH sold AS (
    SELECT product_id, store_id, week_no, sum(quantity) AS units
    FROM dunnhumby.transactions
    GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT
    CASE WHEN p.display = '0' THEN 'not on display' ELSE 'on display' END AS display_status,
    count(*)                                                 AS product_store_weeks_with_sales,
    round(avg(s.units), 2)                                   AS avg_weekly_units,
    round(sum(s.units), 0)                                   AS total_units,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / (SELECT count(*) FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure), 4)
                                                           AS pct_of_all_exposure_rows
FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure p
JOIN sold s USING (product_id, store_id, week_no)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: household_activity_over_time
queries.question: How many households actually shopped, week by week? The panel is fixed at 2,500 households, so what moves is participation, not population.
queries.sql:
-- How many households actually shopped, week by week? The panel is fixed at
-- 2,500 households, so what moves is participation, not population.
SELECT
    week_no,
    count(DISTINCT household_key)                            AS households_shopping,
    count(DISTINCT basket_id)                                 AS baskets,
    count(*)                                                  AS basket_lines,
    round(avg(quantity), 2)                                   AS avg_units_per_line,
    round(sum(gross_sales_value), 2)                          AS gross_sales,
    round(sum(sales_value), 2)                                AS net_sales,
    round(sum(gross_sales_value) / NULLIF(count(DISTINCT basket_id), 0), 2)
                                                           AS avg_basket_value
FROM dunnhumby.transactions
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: household_participation_rate
queries.question: How concentrated is shopping in a few weeks? A panel dataset can look healthy on totals while most households visit only a handful of times all year.
queries.sql:
-- How concentrated is shopping in a few weeks? A panel dataset can look healthy
-- on totals while most households visit only a handful of times all year.
SELECT
    count(*)                                                  AS households_with_basket,
    round(avg(transactions_per_household), 2)                AS avg_transactions,
    min(transactions_per_household)                           AS min_transactions,
    max(transactions_per_household)                           AS max_transactions,
    round(avg(total_spend), 2)                                AS avg_total_spend,
    round(avg(active_days), 2)                                AS avg_active_days,
    round(avg(transactions_per_household) FILTER (WHERE household_key IN (
            SELECT household_key FROM dunnhumby.households)), 2)
                                                           AS avg_tx_households_with_demographics,
    round(avg(transactions_per_household) FILTER (WHERE household_key NOT IN (
            SELECT household_key FROM dunnhumby.households)), 2)
                                                           AS avg_tx_households_without_demographics
FROM (
    SELECT
        household_key,
        count(DISTINCT basket_id) AS transactions_per_household,
        count(DISTINCT day)      AS active_days,
        sum(sales_value)         AS total_spend
    FROM dunnhumby.transactions
    GROUP BY 1
) h;

queries.name: promo_exposure_coverage
queries.question: What share of product-store-weeks were on display or in a mailer. display and mailer are text codes in the source ('0','6','A','D'), not numbers, so they are reported as counts per code rather than summed.
queries.sql:
-- What share of product-store-weeks were on display or in a mailer. display and
-- mailer are text codes in the source ('0','6','A','D'), not numbers, so they
-- are reported as counts per code rather than summed.
SELECT
    display,
    count(*)                                                 AS product_store_weeks,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)       AS pct_of_exposure_rows
FROM dunnhumby.promo_exposure
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC;

queries.name: rfm_segment_value
queries.question: The panel's RFM segmentation. Value per household by segment shows which segment actually carries the panel rather than which is largest.
queries.sql:
-- The panel's RFM segmentation. Value per household by segment shows which
-- segment actually carries the panel rather than which is largest.
SELECT
    classification_3                                         AS segment,
    count(*)                                                  AS households,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)       AS pct_of_households,
    round(avg(recency_days), 2)                              AS avg_recency_days,
    round(avg(frequency), 2)                                 AS avg_frequency,
    round(avg(monetary), 2)                                  AS avg_monetary,
    round(sum(monetary), 2)                                  AS total_monetary,
    round(100.0 * sum(monetary) / sum(sum(monetary)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_panel_value
FROM dunnhumby.household_rfm
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY total_monetary DESC;

queries.name: sales_mix_by_department
queries.question: Which parts of the store carry the business. Department is the top level of the dunnhumby product hierarchy (manufacturer > brand > category > commodity).
queries.sql:
-- Which parts of the store carry the business. Department is the top level of
-- the dunnhumby product hierarchy (manufacturer > brand > category > commodity).
SELECT
    p.department,
    count(DISTINCT p.product_id)                              AS products,
    count(*)                                                  AS basket_lines,
    round(sum(t.quantity), 0)                                 AS units,
    round(sum(t.gross_sales_value), 2)                        AS gross_sales,
    round(sum(t.sales_value), 2)                              AS net_sales,
    round(100.0 * sum(t.sales_value) / sum(sum(t.sales_value)) OVER (), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_net_sales,
    round(sum(t.total_discount), 2)                           AS discount_given,
    round(100.0 * sum(t.total_discount) / sum(t.gross_sales_value), 2)
                                                           AS discount_rate_pct
FROM dunnhumby.transactions t
JOIN dunnhumby.products p USING (product_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY net_sales DESC;

queries.name: demand_scale_by_hierarchy
queries.question: How big is each part of the hierarchy? M5 is famously small on the shelf and huge on volume, so item counts and unit counts are reported together.
queries.sql:
-- How big is each part of the hierarchy? M5 is famously small on the shelf and
-- huge on volume, so item counts and unit counts are reported together.
SELECT
    dept_id,
    cat_id,
    count(DISTINCT id)                                        AS series,
    count(DISTINCT item_id)                                   AS items,
    count(DISTINCT store_id)                                  AS stores,
    round(sum(sales), 0)                                      AS units,
    round(avg(sales), 2)                                      AS avg_units_per_series_day,
    round(100.0 * sum(sales) / sum(sum(sales)) OVER (), 2)   AS pct_of_all_units
FROM m5.sales_long
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY units DESC;

queries.name: event_day_impact
queries.question: M5's calendar flags holidays (Super Bowl, Christmas, Black Friday). This compares flagged days with ordinary ones, which is the first thing a forecaster needs to know about its own calendar feature.
queries.sql:
-- M5's calendar flags holidays (Super Bowl, Christmas, Black Friday). This
-- compares flagged days with ordinary ones, which is the first thing a
-- forecaster needs to know about its own calendar feature.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN c.event_name_1 IS NULL AND c.event_name_2 IS NULL THEN 'no event flagged'
        WHEN c.event_name_1 IS NOT NULL                       THEN 'one event'
        ELSE                                                        'two events'
    END                                                       AS event_count,
    count(*)                                                  AS days,
    round(avg(t.total_units), 0)                              AS avg_units_per_day,
    round(avg(t.total_units) / (
            SELECT avg(total_units) FROM m5.sales_daily_total), 2)
                                                           AS vs_average_day
FROM m5.sales_daily_total t
JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: intermittency
queries.question: The single most important fact for choosing a forecasting method. M5 series are famously intermittent: most series sell zero on most days, so a mean forecast and a naive "same as yesterday" behave very differently here.
queries.sql:
-- The single most important fact for choosing a forecasting method. M5 series
-- are famously intermittent: most series sell zero on most days, so a mean
-- forecast and a naive "same as yesterday" behave very differently here.
SELECT
    count(*)                                                  AS series_days,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales = 0)                         AS zero_sales_days,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales = 0) / count(*), 2)
                                                           AS pct_zero_sales_days,
    round(avg(sales), 3)                                      AS avg_units,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales > 0)                         AS nonzero_sales_days,
    round(avg(sales) FILTER (WHERE sales > 0), 3)             AS avg_units_on_selling_days,
    max(sales)                                                AS max_units_one_day
FROM m5.sales_long;

queries.name: intermittency_by_series
queries.question: Intermittency is not uniform across series, and an aggregate percentage hides that. This buckets each series by the share of days it sold nothing. WITH per_series AS (
queries.sql:
-- Intermittency is not uniform across series, and an aggregate percentage hides
-- that. This buckets each series by the share of days it sold nothing.
WITH per_series AS (
    SELECT
        id,
        count(*)                                   AS days,
        count(*) FILTER (WHERE sales = 0)          AS zero_days,
        sum(sales)                                 AS units
    FROM m5.sales_long
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >= 90 THEN '1. silent 90%+ of days'
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >= 70 THEN '2. silent 70-89% of days'
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >= 40 THEN '3. silent 40-69% of days'
        WHEN 100.0 * zero_days / days >  0  THEN '4. sells something most days'
        ELSE                                      '5. never zero'
    END                                           AS intermittency_band,
    count(*)                                      AS series,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_series,
    round(sum(units), 0)                          AS total_units,
    round(100.0 * sum(units) / sum(sum(units)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_all_units
FROM per_series
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: price_and_demand
queries.question: Does a higher sell price go with lower demand? Prices live in m5.sell_prices per store, item and wm_yr_wk, so the daily facts are first collapsed to the same weekly grain before joining - joining 59 million daily rows to the price table on a daily key that the price table does not have is both wrong and slow. WITH weekly AS (
queries.sql:
-- Does a higher sell price go with lower demand? Prices live in m5.sell_prices
-- per store, item and wm_yr_wk, so the daily facts are first collapsed to the
-- same weekly grain before joining - joining 59 million daily rows to the price
-- table on a daily key that the price table does not have is both wrong and slow.
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT
        s.store_id,
        s.item_id,
        c.wm_yr_wk,
        sum(s.sales) AS units
    FROM m5.sales_long s
    JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
    GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
),
priced AS (
    SELECT
        w.store_id,
        w.item_id,
        w.wm_yr_wk,
        w.units,
        p.sell_price
    FROM weekly w
    JOIN m5.sell_prices p
      ON p.store_id = w.store_id
     AND p.item_id  = w.item_id
     AND p.wm_yr_wk = w.wm_yr_wk
)
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN sell_price <= 0        THEN '1. non-positive price'
        WHEN sell_price <  1        THEN '2. under 1'
        WHEN sell_price <  3        THEN '3. 1 to 3'
        WHEN sell_price <  5        THEN '4. 3 to 5'
        WHEN sell_price <  10       THEN '5. 5 to 10'
        ELSE                             '6. 10 and over'
    END                                               AS price_band,
    count(*)                                          AS item_store_weeks,
    round(avg(sell_price), 2)                         AS avg_price,
    round(avg(units), 2)                              AS avg_weekly_units,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE units = 0) / count(*), 2)
                                                      AS pct_weeks_with_no_sales
FROM priced
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: store_comparison
queries.question: All ten stores carry exactly the same 3,049 series, which makes this a clean like-for-like comparison. CA_3 sells more than double CA_4, so "Walmart demand" is meaningless without naming the store.
queries.sql:
-- All ten stores carry exactly the same 3,049 series, which makes this a clean
-- like-for-like comparison. CA_3 sells more than double CA_4, so "Walmart demand"
-- is meaningless without naming the store.
SELECT
    store_id,
    count(DISTINCT id)                                        AS series,
    round(sum(sales), 0)                                      AS total_units,
    round(100.0 * sum(sales) / sum(sum(sales)) OVER (), 2)   AS pct_of_units,
    round(avg(sales), 3)                                      AS avg_units_per_series_day,
    min(date)                                                 AS first_date,
    max(date)                                                 AS last_date
FROM m5.sales_long
JOIN m5.calendar USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY total_units DESC;

queries.name: weekday_seasonality
queries.question: Retail demand is weekly before it is anything else. This is the weekday seasonality a forecaster has to model, measured on the full daily total rather than on a sample. M5 numbers weekdays from 1 = Saturday.
queries.sql:
-- Retail demand is weekly before it is anything else. This is the weekday
-- seasonality a forecaster has to model, measured on the full daily total rather
-- than on a sample. M5 numbers weekdays from 1 = Saturday.
SELECT
    c.wday,
    c.weekday,
    count(*)                                                  AS days,
    round(avg(t.total_units), 0)                              AS avg_units_per_day,
    min(t.total_units)                                        AS min_units,
    max(t.total_units)                                        AS max_units,
    round(100.0 * sum(t.total_units) / sum(sum(t.total_units)) OVER (), 2)
                                                           AS pct_of_all_units
FROM m5.sales_daily_total t
JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: yearly_trend
queries.question: How did demand move across the 5.4-year window? Any forecast has to start from the level and direction actually observed, not an assumed trend.
queries.sql:
-- How did demand move across the 5.4-year window? Any forecast has to start
-- from the level and direction actually observed, not an assumed trend.
SELECT
    c.year,
    count(*)                                                  AS days,
    round(sum(t.total_units), 0)                              AS total_units,
    round(avg(t.total_units), 0)                              AS avg_units_per_day,
    round(avg(t.total_units) FILTER (WHERE c.wday = 6), 0)   AS avg_saturday_units,
    round(avg(t.total_units) FILTER (WHERE c.wday = 7), 0)   AS avg_sunday_units
FROM m5.sales_daily_total t
JOIN m5.calendar c USING (d_num)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: customer_repeat_behaviour
queries.question: Does anyone come back?
queries.sql:
-- Does anyone come back?
--
-- GROUPING IS THE WHOLE QUESTION HERE. olist.orders.customer_id is the primary
-- key of olist.customers, so it is unique BY CONSTRUCTION - one row per order.
-- Counting distinct customer_id therefore always returns the order count and
-- makes repeat purchasing impossible to see; an earlier draft of this query
-- returned exactly 1.000 orders per customer for that reason alone. The person is
-- identified by customer_unique_id, which repeats across orders.
WITH per_customer AS (
    SELECT
        c.customer_unique_id,
        count(*)                              AS orders,
        count(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', o.purchase_date)) AS active_months
    FROM olist.orders o
    JOIN olist.customers c USING (customer_id)
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    (SELECT count(*) FROM olist.orders)                     AS orders,
    count(*)                                                AS distinct_people,
    round((SELECT count(*) FROM olist.orders)::numeric / count(*), 3)
                                                          AS orders_per_person,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders = 1)                     AS people_ordering_once,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders = 1) / count(*), 2)
                                                          AS pct_people_ordering_once,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 2)                    AS people_ordering_twice_plus,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 2) / count(*), 2)
                                                          AS pct_people_returning,
    max(orders)                                            AS most_orders_by_one_person
FROM per_customer;

queries.name: delay_distribution
queries.question: On-time deliveries are an average; the tail is what generates complaints. This buckets the delivered orders by how far past the estimate they landed.
queries.sql:
-- On-time deliveries are an average; the tail is what generates complaints.
-- This buckets the delivered orders by how far past the estimate they landed.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN delay_days <= 0    THEN '1. on or before estimate'
        WHEN delay_days <= 1    THEN '2. up to 1 day late'
        WHEN delay_days <= 3    THEN '3. 2-3 days late'
        WHEN delay_days <= 7    THEN '4. 4-7 days late'
        WHEN delay_days <= 14   THEN '5. 8-14 days late'
        ELSE                         '6. more than 14 days late'
    END                                                     AS delay_band,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_delivered
FROM olist.orders
WHERE is_delivered AND delay_days IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: delivery_performance
queries.question: How reliable are Olist's delivery promises? Compares what was promised against what actually happened, and separates "late" from "so late it matters". delay_days <= 0 means delivered on or before the estimate.
queries.sql:
-- How reliable are Olist's delivery promises? Compares what was promised against
-- what actually happened, and separates "late" from "so late it matters".
-- delay_days <= 0 means delivered on or before the estimate.
SELECT
    o.is_delivered,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.delay_days <= 0)              AS on_or_before_estimate,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.delay_days <= 0) / count(*), 2)
                                                          AS pct_on_time,
    round(avg(o.delay_days)::numeric, 2)                  AS avg_delay_days,
    round(avg(o.delivery_days)::numeric, 2)               AS avg_delivery_days,
    round(avg(o.estimated_days)::numeric, 2)              AS avg_promised_days,
    round(max(o.delay_days)::numeric, 0)                  AS worst_delay_days
FROM olist.orders o
WHERE o.is_delivered
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1 DESC;

queries.name: geography_revenue_concentration
queries.question: Where is the demand? Uses the order's own destination, not the seller's, and reports how much revenue sits in states with no geolocation mapping at all.
queries.sql:
-- Where is the demand? Uses the order's own destination, not the seller's, and
-- reports how much revenue sits in states with no geolocation mapping at all.
SELECT
    COALESCE(c.customer_state, '(no state)')              AS destination_state,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(sum(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS revenue,
    round(100.0 * sum(a.payment_total) / sum(sum(a.payment_total)) OVER (), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_revenue
FROM olist.orders o
JOIN olist.order_payments_agg a USING (order_id)
LEFT JOIN olist.customers c USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 12;

queries.name: monthly_revenue_trend
queries.question: How did order volume and revenue move month by month across the whole period? Olist is widely described as a high-growth marketplace; the shape of this series is the first thing any dashboard should show. count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id), NOT customer_id: orders.customer_id is the primary key of olist.customers and is unique per order, so counting it here would report the same number of "customers" as orders in every month and make it look as though nobody ever bought twice.
queries.sql:
-- How did order volume and revenue move month by month across the whole period?
-- Olist is widely described as a high-growth marketplace; the shape of this
-- series is the first thing any dashboard should show.
-- count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id), NOT customer_id: orders.customer_id is
-- the primary key of olist.customers and is unique per order, so counting it
-- here would report the same number of "customers" as orders in every month and
-- make it look as though nobody ever bought twice.
SELECT
    to_char(date_trunc('month', o.purchase_date), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id)                  AS customers,
    round(sum(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS revenue,
    round(avg(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS avg_order_value,
    round(sum(a.payment_count), 0)                        AS payment_rows
FROM olist.orders o
JOIN olist.order_payments_agg a USING (order_id)
JOIN olist.customers c USING (customer_id)
WHERE a.payment_total > 0
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: multi_payment_orders
queries.question: Some orders are settled by several payments. This is why order_payments_agg has fewer rows than payments, and why revenue must not be counted per row.
queries.sql:
-- Some orders are settled by several payments. This is why order_payments_agg
-- has fewer rows than payments, and why revenue must not be counted per row.
SELECT
    payment_count                                         AS payments_settling_order,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(payment_total), 2)                          AS revenue,
    round(avg(payment_total), 2)                          AS avg_order_value
FROM olist.order_payments_agg
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: order_status_funnel
queries.question: What actually happened to every order? Revenue is only real once an order reaches a terminal state, so this separates money that was collected from money that was attempted.
queries.sql:
-- What actually happened to every order? Revenue is only real once an order
-- reaches a terminal state, so this separates money that was collected from
-- money that was attempted.
SELECT
    o.order_status,
    count(*)                                              AS orders,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_orders,
    round(sum(a.payment_total), 2)                        AS payment_attempted,
    round(100.0 * sum(a.payment_total) / sum(sum(a.payment_total)) OVER (), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_payment_attempted
FROM olist.orders o
LEFT JOIN olist.order_payments_agg a USING (order_id)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY payment_attempted DESC NULLS LAST;

queries.name: payment_behaviour
queries.question: How do customers actually pay? Installments are the interesting column: a single R$100 payment in 1 instalment and in 10 are different products.
queries.sql:
-- How do customers actually pay? Installments are the interesting column: a
-- single R$100 payment in 1 instalment and in 10 are different products.
SELECT
    p.payment_type,
    count(*)                                              AS payment_rows,
    round(sum(p.payment_value), 2)                        AS value,
    round(100.0 * sum(p.payment_value) / sum(sum(p.payment_value)) OVER (), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_all_value,
    round(avg(p.payment_installments), 2)                 AS avg_installments,
    max(p.payment_installments)                           AS max_installments,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1)    AS rows_on_installments,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1)
          / count(*), 2)                                  AS pct_rows_on_installments,
    round(sum(p.payment_value) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1), 2)
                                                          AS value_on_installments,
    round(100.0 * sum(p.payment_value) FILTER (WHERE p.payment_installments > 1)
          / sum(p.payment_value), 2)                      AS pct_of_type_value_on_installments
FROM olist.payments p
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY value DESC;

queries.name: review_coverage_and_score
queries.question: Only customers who were happy enough to write can be measured at all, so this reports review COVERAGE before it reports score. A 4.5 average over 6% of orders is a very different claim from a 4.5 average over 90%. DISTINCT is required, not decorative: olist.reviews holds more review rows than there are reviewed orders, so a plain count(*) over this join counts a multi-review order several times and inflates the coverage rate.
queries.sql:
-- Only customers who were happy enough to write can be measured at all, so this
-- reports review COVERAGE before it reports score. A 4.5 average over 6% of
-- orders is a very different claim from a 4.5 average over 90%.
-- DISTINCT is required, not decorative: olist.reviews holds more review rows
-- than there are reviewed orders, so a plain count(*) over this join counts a
-- multi-review order several times and inflates the coverage rate.
SELECT
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id)                            AS orders_total,
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE r.order_id IS NOT NULL)
                                                          AS orders_with_review,
    count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE r.order_id IS NULL)
                                                          AS orders_without_review,
    round(100.0 * count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE r.order_id IS NOT NULL)
          / count(DISTINCT o.order_id), 2)                AS pct_reviewed,
    round(avg(r.review_score), 2)                         AS avg_score_across_reviews,
    min(r.review_score)                                   AS min_score,
    max(r.review_score)                                   AS max_score,
    count(DISTINCT r.review_id)                           AS distinct_review_ids,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.review_id IS NOT NULL)       AS review_rows
FROM olist.orders o
LEFT JOIN olist.reviews r USING (order_id);

queries.name: review_grain_candidates
queries.question: Which key actually holds? Tests the three plausible grains rather than asserting one. rows - distinct pairs is the surplus; zero means the key is a valid primary key.
queries.sql:
-- Which key actually holds? Tests the three plausible grains rather than
-- asserting one. rows - distinct pairs is the surplus; zero means the key is a
-- valid primary key.
SELECT 'review_id alone'   AS candidate_key, '1 row per review'        AS claimed_grain,
       count(*) - count(DISTINCT review_id) AS surplus_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE review_id IS NULL) AS null_rows
FROM olist.reviews
UNION ALL
SELECT 'review_id + order_id', '1 row per review-per-order link',
       count(*) - count(DISTINCT (review_id, order_id)),
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE review_id IS NULL OR order_id IS NULL)
FROM olist.reviews
UNION ALL
SELECT 'order_id + review_creation_date', '1 row per order, repeated reviews impossible',
       count(*) - count(DISTINCT (order_id, review_creation_date)),
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE order_id IS NULL OR review_creation_date IS NULL)
FROM olist.reviews
ORDER BY surplus_rows;
rows: 1 row per order, repeated reviews impossible

queries.name: review_id_forensics
queries.question: WHY review_id IS NOT A PRIMARY KEY HERE
queries.sql:
-- WHY review_id IS NOT A PRIMARY KEY HERE
--
-- review_id repeats: 99,224 rows carry only 98,410 distinct values. The obvious
-- reading is that a customer re-submitted the same review, but the evidence says
-- something else entirely. This query lays out the test, one row per duplicated
-- review_id.
--
-- The discriminator is the timestamp. A genuine re-submission is a second event
-- and would carry its own creation and answer times. If every duplicated row
-- shares both timestamps exactly, there was only ever ONE review, and the
-- dataset is repeating it across several of that customer's orders.
--
-- The second column, orders_placed_after_the_review, is the clincher. A customer
-- cannot review an order they had not yet placed, so any row where it happens
-- proves the association was manufactured rather than reported.
WITH duplicated AS (
    SELECT review_id, count(*) AS rows_in_group
    FROM olist.reviews
    GROUP BY 1
    HAVING count(*) > 1
),
per_review AS (
    SELECT
        r.review_id,
        max(d.rows_in_group)                                    AS rows_in_group,
        count(DISTINCT r.order_id)                               AS distinct_orders,
        count(DISTINCT c.customer_unique_id)                     AS distinct_people,
        count(DISTINCT r.review_score)                           AS distinct_scores,
        -- coalesce matters: most reviews carry no title at all, and
        -- count(DISTINCT review_comment_title) ignores NULLs, so it would
        -- report 0 distinct titles for a group and make "all the same" look
        -- false when it is merely absent.
        count(DISTINCT coalesce(r.review_comment_title, '<none>'))   AS distinct_titles,
        count(DISTINCT coalesce(r.review_comment_message, '<none>')) AS distinct_messages,
        count(DISTINCT r.review_creation_date)                   AS distinct_creation_dates,
        count(DISTINCT r.review_answer_timestamp)                AS distinct_answer_dates,
        count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.purchase_date > r.review_creation_date)
                                                               AS orders_placed_after_the_review,
        count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)                            AS customer_rows_behind_the_orders
    FROM olist.reviews r
    JOIN duplicated d ON d.review_id = r.review_id
    JOIN olist.orders o    ON o.order_id = r.order_id
    JOIN olist.customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    rows_in_group,
    count(*)                                                     AS review_ids,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_people = 1)                  AS all_one_person,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_scores = 1)                  AS all_same_score,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_titles = 1 AND distinct_messages = 1)
                                                                 AS all_same_text,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE distinct_creation_dates = 1 AND distinct_answer_dates = 1)
                                                                 AS all_same_both_timestamps,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders_placed_after_the_review > 0)   AS impossible_chronology,
    sum(distinct_orders)                                         AS order_links,
    sum(orders_placed_after_the_review)                          AS impossible_order_links
FROM per_review
-- GROUPING SETS adds an "all" row so the totals are measured rather than
-- summed by hand in the write-up.
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((rows_in_group), ())
ORDER BY rows_in_group NULLS LAST;

queries.name: review_score_distribution
queries.question: Score distribution alongside the comment volume behind each score. A 1-star with no comment is a different event from a 1-star with a paragraph.
queries.sql:
-- Score distribution alongside the comment volume behind each score. A 1-star
-- with no comment is a different event from a 1-star with a paragraph.
SELECT
    r.review_score,
    count(*)                                              AS reviews,
    round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2)     AS pct_of_reviews,
    round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.review_comment_message IS NOT NULL)
          / count(*), 2)                                  AS pct_with_comment,
    round(avg(length(r.review_comment_message)), 0)       AS avg_comment_chars
FROM olist.reviews r
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

queries.name: seller_concentration
queries.question: How dependent is the marketplace on its biggest sellers? This measures gross merchandise value as the SUM OF order_items.item_total, NOT the order's payment_total: an order with six items has six rows, so joining items to payments and summing the order total would count that order's revenue six times. Each item belongs to exactly one seller, so item-level GMV cannot double-count. WITH seller_gmv AS (
queries.sql:
-- How dependent is the marketplace on its biggest sellers? This measures gross
-- merchandise value as the SUM OF order_items.item_total, NOT the order's
-- payment_total: an order with six items has six rows, so joining items to
-- payments and summing the order total would count that order's revenue six
-- times. Each item belongs to exactly one seller, so item-level GMV cannot
-- double-count.
WITH seller_gmv AS (
    SELECT
        i.seller_id,
        count(DISTINCT i.order_id) AS orders,
        sum(i.item_total)          AS gmv
    FROM olist.order_items i
    GROUP BY 1
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        row_number() OVER (ORDER BY gmv DESC) AS seller_rank,
        orders,
        gmv
    FROM seller_gmv
),
thresholds(n) AS (VALUES (1), (10), (50), (100), (500), (1000), (3095))
SELECT
    t.n                                                   AS top_n_sellers,
    round(100.0 * t.n / (SELECT count(*) FROM seller_gmv), 2) AS pct_of_sellers,
    count(*)                                              AS sellers_cumulative,
    -- An order with items from three sellers is counted once per seller, so this
    -- is (seller, order) pairs, not distinct orders.
    sum(r.orders)                                         AS seller_order_pairs,
    round(sum(r.gmv), 2)                                  AS gmv_cumulative,
    round(100.0 * sum(r.gmv) / (SELECT sum(gmv) FROM seller_gmv), 2)
                                                          AS pct_of_gmv
FROM thresholds t
JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_rank <= t.n
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;
